newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania coffee output seen declining, quality up.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania coffee output seen declining, quality up.

text.p: Tanzania's coffee output and earnings are set for a sharp fall for the 1996/97 season but crop quality is improving, authorities said on Wednesday.
"This year (1996/97) we are expecting a much lower crop at a much reduced price but (coffee) quality has improved," said Edward Sannda, Tanzania Coffee Board Managing Director.
Sannda forecast production in the current season at between 41,000 and 43,000 tonnes, worth an estimated $90 million.
This compared with 1995/96 output of 53,000 tonnes which earned about $115 million, and around 44,000 tonnes in 1994/95 worth $139 million.
He told Reuters that auctions of the new coffee crop had started in August and were held every two weeks. Exporters could pay in either dollars or Tanzanian shillings.

Following a meeting between the coffee board, coffee exporters and growers on August 20, a dispute over the method of payment had been resolved and auctions had resumed in the northern coffee town of Moshi under the new dual payment system on September 1.

"Basically, it was resolved that the exporter can pay in dollars or in Tanzanian shillings. If he (exporter) pays in dollars, then he pays in dollars at the quoted selling rate (invoice value). If he opts to pay in Tanzanian shillings, then he must pay at the ruling selling rate of that day," he said.
Sannda said there had been no sales in Tanzania by private treaty for seven years.
He said the overall quality of Tanzanian coffee was improving and this was reflected in strong demand from Far Eastern and European buyers.

A grower education project involving 30 ministry of agriculture experts advising smallholders on the latest farming techniques was having a positive impact on improving overall coffee quality, Sannda said.
Yields for coffee production in Tanzania are among the lowest in the world, averaging 200-300 kg per hectare, due mostly to the age of the coffee trees, in some areas more than 100 years old.
Moshi-based Jeremy Lefroy, Managing Director of the Africa Coffee Co, agreed that the problem of coffee trees well past their prime years was a key factor in declining production.
However, despite slumping production this year, Lefroy said Tanzanian coffee was doing reasonably well at international auctions and quality was improving.

"Tanzania actually gets very good prices compared to the world market," Lefroy told Reuters, adding that Tanzanian mild washed arabicas were selling at New York auctions at prices only exceeded by Kenya and Colombia.
Africa Coffee Co trades between 3,000 and 4,000 tonnes of Tanzanian coffee, mostly arabica, a year, Lefroy said.
